text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementHistoryWhat Public Health Initiatives Looked Like in the Middle AgesThe road to hell is paved in good intentions, the roads in Trondheim were paved in something elseJCBy Jake Currie3:00 PM CST on November 13, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleMedieval Europe isn’t exactly known for its major advances in public health, but a new book is challenging those assumptions. In it, the authors take a multidisciplinary approach to better understand how the citizens of Trondheim, an ancient Norwegian city, grappled with growing concerns about illnesses.   Powered By 1061.7K 30ShareNextStayTrondheim’s population exploded in the Early Middle Ages, increasing from roughly 250 around 950 CE to 1,500 by the 12th century, then doubling during the High Middle Ages to about 3,000. It was during this period that monks and other scholars arrived, including the archbishop. With them, they brought new theories of disease spread, notably the miasma theory that illnesses were spread by foul odors. Read more: “The Medieval Friar Who Foretold Carl Sagan’s “Star-Stuff””Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisement
